newsitem.title: USA: Delta signs exclusive pact with Boeing.
newsitem.headline: Delta signs exclusive pact with Boeing.

text.p: Delta Air Lines Inc said it signed an exclusive supply pact with Boeing Co that will cover its aircraft acquisition needs for the next 20 to 25 years.

The Atlanta-based carrier said it ordered 106 Boeing aircraft and has options for 124 more in a deal valued at $15 billion. The plan also includes "rolling options" for 414 aircraft, bringing the potential deal to 644 planes.
Options are guaranteed delivery slots. Rolling options are a pool of aircraft delivery positions that replace options as the options expire or are exercised.
The deal includes firm base-pricing on the firm orders, options and rolling options aircraft.
Delta had been in intense negotiations with both Boeing and Airbus Industrie for several months. Boeing, however, was the clear winner on initial start-up costs and order flexibility, Delta said.

Committing to a single manufacturer allows Delta to streamline its fleet, reduce maintenance and training costs. The plan will also allow Delta to retire its older aircraft, lowering operational costs.

Delta said it plans to maintain the ability to pay for the aircraft with internally-generated funds, while still meeting financial goals for annual operating margins, a lower debt structure and a solidly investment grade debt rating.
Delta said the plan is based on internal capacity growth of about two percent a year through 2002.
Two percent growth is in line with expected growth demand for the airline industry, Delta said. Beyond 2002, the fleet plan is very flexible, Delta said.

The deal allows Delta to manage its capacity growth by timing the delivery of both firm and option aircraft in line with competitive, economic and market conditions. The agreement also allows Delta to switch orders from wide-bodied aircraft to narrow-bodied, or vice versa.

"This flexible and disciplined fleet acquisition plan gives us the right aircraft at the right time and at the right price to build on Delta's competitive advantages as we put our global strategy in place," said Delta Chairman Ronald Allen.
"We can manage deliveries while providing significant long-term price control," Allen said.
Delta said the aircraft plan concentrates on domestic aircraft, but it will continue to evaluate its international aircraft needs.
The plan does not include firm orders for the Boeing 777 wide-bodied aircraft, but Delta negotiated options on 777s at a fixed base price.
The aircraft order will make Delta the first airline to launch Boeing's 767-400, the next generation in the 767 wide-bodied line.
Delta said it remains in talks with aircraft engine manufacturers for engines to power the new fleet.
